newsitem.title: GERMANY: Focus-EMI slams EU for dragging heels on budgets.
newsitem.headline: Focus-EMI slams EU for dragging heels on budgets.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute (EMI) on Tuesday expressed serious concern that many EU states have not yet managed to rein in their national deficits enough to launch the euro as planned in January 1999.

The forerunner of the European Central Bank warned countries against using one-off tricks to create a better budgetary picture, but said "durable" action had to be taken to ensure a successful move to a single European currency.
"On the fiscal side, the situation remains far from satisfactory in many countries," EMI President Alexandre Lamfalussy wrote in a foreword to the EMI's annual report.
"Despite efforts made at consolidation, which have contributed to a fall in actual deficits, the latter still overshoot the reference values laid down in the Treaty in most countries," he added.
The stern tone of the report came as no surprise to analysts, who had expected the EMI to take a hard line on the EU's dismal record on debt control.
"If monetary union were left purely down to the EMI, then you could say this report is bad news for the broad EMU story," said Darren Wiliams, European economist at UBS in London.
Only about one year remains before the European Commission reaches a final decision, based on 1997 data, as to which EU states qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU).

A key Maastricht Treaty clause calls for national debts to total no more than 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) -- or to show significant progress in falling toward this level -- and for budget deficits to be three percent or less.

But statistics compiled by the EMI, which date from autumn 1996, showed an overall EU debt position of 73.5 percent of GDP and a deficit level of 4.4 percent, well over target. Germany, the linchpin of the euro project and the third best performer on price stability, had a deficit rate of four percent.
The report, said analysts, was a clear reminder that EMU entry is not a foregone conclusion for all euro hopefuls, especially "Club Med" states which lack a history of fiscal discipline.

"This is good news for Germany," said Joerg Kraemer, economist at Merrill Lynch, Frankfurt. "We think Germany will miss the deficit target by 0.4 percent. But it is good news nevertheless because Germany has quite a solid underlying fiscal performance."

Lamfalussy said that clear progress had been made toward harmonising inflation and bond yields, the other key issues for preparing for the planned euro launch in 1999, and that exchange rate stability had been broadly maintained.
But more efforts were needed in the coming months -- the decisive period for convincing markets that Europe's new anchor currency will be as stable as the deutschemark.
"Setbacks in the consolidation of public finances or other factors that may reduce confidence in the EMU process may negatively affect financial markets," the report cautioned.

Lamfalussy said countries were relying too much on boosting revenue to reduce deficits rather than cutting spending. "Furthermore, sustainable consolidation cannot be achieved by one-off or accounting measures."
The outlook for low inflation throughout the EU region was good, the EMI said, but central banks would have to remain particularly alert to inflation risks in the period ahead.

"The stance adopted in the period ahead will be particularly important in that it will increasingly affect inflation in 1999 and thereafter and hence price expectations for the euro area," the report said.
The EMI also urged more action to reform Europe's sluggish jobs market and said efforts so far to create more flexible working conditions in the region had proved inadequate.

Noting that employment had barely risen in the region since the cyclical trough of 1993, Lamfalussy said: "Unemployment trends are...extremely worrisome; in my view the recent record of the Union in terms of job creation is dismal."

As had been widely expected, the EMI's report steered carefully clear of the most controversial political EMU issues, such as which countries are likely to qualify for the 1999 start and whether a delayed launch might be conceivable.

These questions, along with the question of how precisely Maastricht convergence criteria must be fulfilled, have become hot issues as more and more signs emerge that even Europe's economic powerhouses are struggling to make the EMU grade.

Nor did the EMI, whose main task is preparing the ground for the ECB when it starts operations next year, shed more light on monetary policy strategies for the euro zone, although it said it would release more information in 1997.

The framework is in place for the ECB to choose from a variety of policy scenarios, such as whether to base policy decisions on a direct inflation indicator or on money supply trends, a lagging indicator of price developments.
